lessons.contracts__ijara:
When you rent something, you're not buying the thing itself — you're paying to use it for a while. Say you rent a bike for the weekend. The bike still belongs to the shop. You didn't buy a bike, you bought the right to ride it for two days.

Because the bike still belongs to the shop, the shop carries the owner's risks. If the bike breaks down through no fault of yours — the chain just snaps from being old — that's the shop's loss, not yours. Your payments stop. But if you're the one who crashed it into a wall, that damage is on you. Basic upkeep and big repairs are the owner's job; you're only responsible for normal use and for any mess you personally cause.

This is exactly what separates real renting from a loan pretending to be a rental. If the deal says you have to keep paying no matter what — even if the bike gets stolen or totally wrecked with no fault of yours — then the shop isn't actually carrying any risk anymore. It's not really a rental anymore either, even if everyone calls it one.

Sometimes a rental is designed so that at the end, ownership passes to the renter — like renting a laptop for a year and then it becomes yours. This can replace things like a loan for a house or a car. But scholars insist on one condition: the promise to hand over ownership at the end has to be a separate promise, not baked into the rental payments themselves. Otherwise the two deals blur together, and it quietly turns into "buying in installments" dressed up as a rental.

Charging extra as a percentage for paying late isn't allowed in renting either, for the same reason it isn't allowed in the buy-resell deals we looked at before.

One more thing worth remembering — and this isn't just about renting objects like bikes or laptops. It's also about hiring people to do work for you, like paying someone to mow your lawn or tutor you. There's a hadith where the Prophet ﷺ says he will personally be an opponent, on Judgment Day, against three kinds of people — and one of them is someone who hired a worker, got the full work done, and then didn't pay them what was owed. Renting things and paying people fairly for their work are part of the same idea.
lessons.contracts__mudaraba-musharaka:
Imagine two ways friends can team up to make money instead of one friend lending the other money with interest.

**Mudaraba** works like this: one person puts in the money, the other puts in the work. Say your older cousin has savings and you have a great idea for a small business — maybe fixing phones. Your cousin gives the capital, you run the business. Before you start, you agree how to split any profit — say sixty percent to you, forty to your cousin. If the business actually makes money, you both gain. But if it loses money, your cousin loses the cash, and you lose all the time and effort you put in — nobody owes anybody anything extra. That's fair, because nobody knew for sure it would work. The only exception: if you lost the money because you were careless or broke the agreed rules, then it's on you to cover it.

**Musharaka** is when both people put in money and both can help run things. Say you and a friend each chip in savings to buy something you can resell. You don't have to split the profit exactly by how much each of you put in — if you also do more of the work, you can agree you get a bigger share of the profit. But if there's a loss, that has to be split exactly according to how much each person invested. No negotiating that part.

Here's the one rule that keeps this whole idea honest: you can agree on a *share* of the profit, but never on a *fixed amount*. The moment someone is guaranteed a set payout no matter what happens, the risk disappears — and it quietly turns into the same thing as a loan with interest, just wearing a different name. That's also why one partner can never promise to just hand the other their money back no matter what.

There's a real-life version of this used instead of a mortgage, called **diminishing partnership**. A bank and a person buy a house together — say the bank owns eighty percent and the person owns twenty. The person lives in the house and pays rent on the bank's share, while also slowly buying more of that share bit by bit. As their share grows, the rent they owe shrinks, until eventually the whole house is theirs.

There's a hadith that says Allah is "the third partner between two partners, as long as neither betrays the other — but when one betrays, He withdraws from them." It shows how much weight honesty carries in a partnership — it's not just a business deal, it's something Allah is watching over.
lessons.contracts__murabaha:
Imagine you want a new phone, but you don't have all the money yet. A bank offers to help — but not by just lending you cash with interest, which would be riba, and that's not allowed. Instead, they use something called murabaha.

Here's how it works. The bank actually buys the phone first. For a little while, the phone belongs to them, not you. Then they sell it to you for the price they paid, plus an extra amount on top — and they tell you exactly what that extra amount is. You then pay them back a little at a time.

For this to count as murabaha, three things have to be true.

- **The bank really owns the phone first.** Not just on paper — really. If the phone got lost or broken before they sold it to you, that would be their problem, not yours. That's what makes it a real sale of something they own, instead of selling something they don't actually have.
- **The extra amount is announced openly.** You know exactly how much the phone cost the bank and exactly how much extra you're paying. Nothing hidden.
- **The price is fixed once and never grows.** Even if you're late paying, the total amount doesn't creep upward. If it did, that would turn back into riba, no matter what the deal is called.

Now, some people point out a real problem: what if the bank owns the phone for like two minutes, just to check a box, and it's not a real, meaningful ownership? Then this starts looking exactly like a regular loan with interest, just wearing a costume. Some scholars say this openly, and it's a genuine, ongoing disagreement in the field — not something this lesson can settle for you.

What if you're late paying? You can't just add more to the bill — that would be riba again. So instead, there can be an agreed fixed penalty, but that money doesn't go into the bank's pocket — it goes to charity. That way, being late still has a consequence, but the bank isn't profiting from your hard time. And the Quran is direct about this: if someone is struggling to pay, give them more time.
lessons.contracts__salam-istisna:
Here's a rule you already sort of know: you can't sell something you don't actually have. That's the basic principle. But there are two special, allowed exceptions — and both exist because someone genuinely needs help, not because someone's trying to trick another person.

**The first is called salam.** Imagine your neighbor grows strawberries. In spring she needs money to buy seeds and pay for water, but she won't have strawberries to sell until summer. So you pay her now, in full, and she promises to give you a set amount of strawberries — a known quantity, a known quality — on an agreed date later.

This only works if a few things are true: you pay the whole amount right away (not half now, half later — that would just turn into a confusing debt-for-debt swap, which isn't allowed), and everyone agrees exactly what's being delivered and when. The strawberries have to be described clearly enough — "this variety, this quality" — not some one-of-a-kind thing that can't be replaced if something goes wrong.

Why bother with this at all? Because it genuinely helps. The grower gets cash when she needs it, without borrowing money and paying interest on it. You, as the buyer, usually pay a bit less than what the strawberries will cost at harvest time — but you're also taking a real risk. Maybe the harvest fails. Maybe prices drop by summer. That risk is shared between you two, not dumped entirely on the person who needed help in the first place.

**The second exception is istisna.** This is for ordering something that doesn't exist yet and has to be *built* — think of commissioning a custom skateboard ramp, or a company ordering a batch of machines. It's similar to salam, but with two differences: you don't have to pay everything upfront — you can pay in stages, as the work progresses. And the timeline can be more flexible — what matters most is that the item and its specifications are crystal clear.

This is why istisna shows up in things like construction projects: the customer pays as each stage is finished, the builder makes exactly what was specified, and both sides are involved in real work being done — not just money moving around.

**One thing both exceptions share:** the thing being paid for has to be described so precisely that if there's ever a disagreement — "wait, this isn't what I ordered" — it can actually be settled by checking the description. That precision is exactly what removes the uncertainty (*gharar*) we talked about earlier in this module. No guessing games, no vague promises — just clear terms everyone agreed to from the start.
lessons.contracts__why-contract:
Imagine someone offers you a deal and says "don't worry, it's totally fair" — but doesn't tell you the details. Would you trust the label, or would you ask questions first? That's exactly the point here. The word "Islamic" stuck on a product doesn't prove anything by itself. What actually matters is how the deal is built, and you can check that with one question: who carries the risk if something goes wrong?

Three things make a deal unfair, and almost every rule grows out of avoiding them:

- Riba — making guaranteed profit from a debt, without any real risk.
- Gharar — too much unclear stuff: nobody really knows what's being sold, for how much, or when.
- Maisir — a bet where one person's win is automatically someone else's loss.

From these three, a few practical rules follow.

You can't sell what you don't actually own. Say a friend wants to buy your bike, but it's not yours yet — your cousin promised to give it to you next week. You can't sell it now, because if it gets stolen before you even have it, whose loss is that? The seller has to actually hold the thing and carry that risk. This is why real Islamic finance deals involve buying and selling actual stuff, not just handing over money and charging for the wait.

The item and the price need to be clear. If you lend your friend some pocket money, "pay me back sometime, some amount" isn't good enough. The longest verse in the Quran is entirely about writing debts down clearly — the amount, and the deadline. That's not a small detail; it's treated as its own important instruction.

Honesty matters more than getting a better price. There's a hadith about two people making a deal: as long as they haven't walked away yet, either can back out. If both were honest and explained things clearly, their deal is blessed. If they lied or hid something, that blessing is wiped out. So if you're trading a game, a toy, or splitting a gift with a sibling, saying exactly what's wrong or missing with it isn't just "nice" — it's the whole point.

Whatever you both agreed to counts. If you and a friend set specific conditions for a deal, you're expected to actually stick to them.

So here's how to look at any money product, even a fancy one with a bank card and an app: don't ask what it's called. Ask what's actually being sold, who owned it at each moment, and who loses out if it's destroyed or goes wrong. Those three questions tell you far more than any label ever could.
lessons.halal-income__crypto:
Crypto is one of those topics where honest people who study Islam carefully still disagree. Not about small stuff — about the big question itself: is crypto even "property" in the same way a toy, a bike, or money in your jar is property?

Some scholars say yes. Their thinking: property just means something people see as valuable and useful, and clearly people treat crypto that way — they trade it, price it, use it. Buying and selling it on the spot isn't so different from swapping one country's currency for another at the airport.

Other scholars say no. Their point: crypto has no real backing — no factory, no crops, no gold behind it — and its price often just moves with people's excitement or fear. That kind of extreme unpredictability worries them, because Islam is careful about deals where nobody really knows what they're getting (this is called gharar). They also point out that a lot of crypto trading looks more like betting on price swings than actually using something — closer to gambling (maysir) than to trade.

Here's the useful part, though: you don't have to solve that debate to know where some clear lines are. A few things are off-limits no matter which side turns out to be right:

- If someone promises you a fixed extra amount just for lending them your money or crypto — like "give me 100 now, I'll give you 110 back guaranteed" — that's the same as interest (riba), whatever the asset is.
- Trading with borrowed money to make bigger bets (leverage), or betting on whether a price will go up or down (futures, options) — these are built on uncertainty and gambling-like risk, so they're not okay.
- If a crypto project's actual business is gambling, something indecent, or lending at interest, it's rejected for what it does — same as any regular company doing those things would be.
- If you're saving crypto the way you'd save money in a jar, and you owe zakat, it counts toward your zakat calculation using its market value on the day you calculate — at least according to the scholars who do treat it as property.

This is exactly why AM Network never launched its own crypto coin, even though that would've been an easy way to raise money. A coin whose value depends purely on people's hopes and hype has that same uncertainty and gambling problem. Instead, AM earns money the honest, clear way: a stated fee for a real service — between 1% and 2.5% per transaction. The blockchain is just used like a notebook where every entry can be checked, not as a way to create a speculative coin.

If you or your family already hold some crypto, this lesson can show you where the clear red lines are — but the deeper question of what crypto *is* isn't something this lesson can settle for you. That's worth asking a knowledgeable, trustworthy scholar directly, rather than deciding from an article.
lessons.halal-income__halal-basics:
Money doesn't become halal just because it's a big amount, or because the job title sounds impressive. What actually matters is three things: what you're selling, how you got the money, and what conditions were attached to the deal.

**First, the thing itself.** If what's being sold is forbidden, it doesn't matter how honestly you sell it. Say a classmate asks you to help resell something like vapes or run a betting pool for a game — doing it "fairly" doesn't fix the problem. The item itself is the issue.

**Second, the method.** Imagine you're selling your old bike to a friend. If you hide a cracked frame, or you count out change wrong on purpose when someone pays you, that money you gained through the trick is not clean — even though selling a bike is completely fine. The Quran is clear that people shouldn't eat away at each other's property unfairly, but trade based on mutual agreement is the exception. Lying about weight, hiding a flaw, taking what isn't yours, or slipping someone a bribe — all of that taints the money, even if the product itself was allowed.

**Third, the agreement.** Even something totally permitted can be ruined by bad terms. If your friend "lends" you $10 but you have to pay back $12, that's interest, and it's not allowed — even though money itself is fine to lend. Same with deals that are basically just gambling in disguise: one person's win is built entirely on the other person's loss.

**What about the grey area?**
Between clearly allowed and clearly forbidden, there's a middle zone — things that aren't obviously one or the other. The Prophet ﷺ said that the allowed is clear and the forbidden is clear, but between them are unclear matters that many people don't know about. Whoever stays away from the unclear things protects their faith and their reputation. This isn't about being paranoid over every dollar. It's simple: if you're not sure, find out — and until you do, don't rush in.

**Why this actually matters.**
There's a hadith about a traveler, worn out and dusty from a long journey, lifting his hands to the sky and calling out to God — but his food was forbidden, his drink was forbidden, his clothes were forbidden, he was raised on forbidden earnings. And the question asked is: how could he possibly expect an answer? Where your money comes from isn't just about your wallet. It follows you.

There's also a warning that feels very modern: a time will come when people stop caring whether what they take is from something allowed or something forbidden. Paying attention to where your money comes from — that's exactly what's being asked of us, whether it's pocket money, a gift from a relative, or your first bit of savings in a jar or on a card.
lessons.halal-income__savings-takaful:
Let's say you and your friends decide to save money in a jar. But there are two very different ways this could work.

Imagine you pay a company a bit of your allowance every month, and in return they promise: if something bad happens — you lose your phone, you get hurt — they'll pay you back. Sounds fair, right? But scholars point out three problems with this ordinary kind of insurance:

- You don't know what you'll get. You might pay for twenty years and never need a payout. Or you might pay once and get a huge sum. That uncertainty about the deal itself is a problem — the same kind of uncertainty as selling something without knowing exactly what you're getting.
- It works like a bet. One side's gain is the other side's loss — you winning big means the company loses, and the other way around. That's the same logic as gambling.
- The company usually invests all that collected money in interest-based stuff, which is its own separate issue.

Now imagine a different setup: you and your friends all put money into a shared jar, but not to "buy" anything — you put it in as a gift, to help whichever one of you needs it later. Nobody's trying to win against anyone else. If your friend's phone breaks, the jar helps pay for it, because that's what you all agreed to do for each other. Someone might volunteer to manage the jar — count the money, keep it organized — and they get paid a fair fee for that job, or a fair cut if the money in the jar earns something. But the jar itself never belongs to them, and if there's extra money left at the end, it goes back to you, not into the manager's pocket.

This second model is called takaful. The difference isn't just the name — it's about who actually owns the money and why people are putting it in. It's built on the idea the Quran teaches, of people helping each other in good and righteous ways.

Worth being honest about: takaful is a modern solution that scholars worked out in the last century to solve this problem — it's not something written out directly in the old texts. Different companies run it differently, so if this ever matters for you or your family, the actual contract needs to be checked, not just the label on it.

There's also stuff like car insurance or health insurance that a country's law simply requires you to have. Scholars discuss that separately, under the idea that you're not blamed for something the law forces on you and you truly can't avoid.

Now, quickly, about saving money in general. Good options: a bank account that doesn't pay you interest, an account that shares real profit with you (called mudaraba), actual gold or silver, or owning a small part of a real business. Not okay: a savings account that pays you interest, no matter what fancy name the bank gives it.

And one more thing to remember — whatever you save, in any of the allowed forms, counts when it's time to calculate zakat.
lessons.halal-income__screening:
When you buy a share, you're not just buying a piece of paper — you're becoming a tiny owner of a real company. That means you share responsibility for what that company actually does. So checking a share happens in two steps.

Step one: what does the company do? Some businesses are out immediately, no matter how good the numbers look — companies whose main business is alcohol, pork, tobacco, gambling and lotteries, indecent content, or interest-based banks and commercial insurance companies. Those last two aren't "borderline" — their whole income is built on interest, so they're excluded from the start.

Step two: how is the company's money handled? Here's the tricky part — almost every big company keeps some cash in interest-bearing accounts or has some loans. Imagine trying to find a company that's never touched a jar with a single coin of interest in it — nearly impossible. So scholars who specialize in this set acceptable limits. One well-known standard (AAOIFI No. 21) uses three checks:

- interest-based debt should be below 30% of the company's market value
- interest-based deposits and investments should be below 30%
- income from forbidden activities should be below 5% of total income

Two honest things to say here. First, this 30/30/5 standard is a modern expert tool, not something written in revelation itself. Second, different providers calculate it differently — some divide by market value, some by total assets, and thresholds shift too. So a company might pass one standard and fail another. That's not a mistake — it's just two careful methods disagreeing.

Now, cleaning the income. If a company has a small slice of forbidden income within these allowed limits, that same slice of your dividends isn't really yours. You work out that portion and give it away for public good — not as charity you're rewarded for, but simply as cleaning your own money.

One more practical point: shares you're holding as savings count toward zakat, the yearly giving on wealth you own. Scholars split this into two cases: shares bought to be resold soon are counted at their full market price, while shares held just to collect dividends are counted, in the view of many, based on your share of the company's liquid, spendable assets.
lessons.riba__riba-today:
Let's find riba in everyday things a teenager might actually see around them.

The rule to remember: riba happens when extra money is charged just for time — not for a product, not for work, not for sharing risk. If you spot that pattern, you've spotted riba.

**A bank card.** Having a card isn't riba by itself. The problem is if you don't pay back what you spent, and the bank adds extra on top just because time passed. Pay it all back before that extra kicks in, and no riba happens there. There's still a separate question about the agreement behind the card allowing that extra charge in the first place — scholars don't all see that the same way.

**A loan for something like a phone or a car**, where you end up paying back more than you borrowed just because you took time to repay — that's riba in its plainest form.

**Savings that earn interest.** Imagine you keep money in a jar, but instead of a jar, it's in a bank account that adds a little extra to your balance every month just for sitting there. That extra is riba too — you're just on the receiving end instead of the paying end.

**Paying in installments**, like splitting the cost of new shoes into monthly payments. If the seller sets one fixed total price up front — even if it's higher than the cash price — most scholars say that's just normal selling, since the seller priced the delay in once and it doesn't change. But if the amount grows because you paid late, or extra gets added onto what you still owe, that's riba.

**A house loan (mortgage).** The regular kind with interest falls under riba. There's a real difference of opinion among scholars about what to do if someone lives somewhere with no Islamic alternative available — some allow it in real necessity, others don't. This isn't something to decide from an article; it needs a knowledgeable scholar who knows the actual situation.

**Late fees.** If a fee keeps growing the longer you're late, that's riba. A one-time fixed fee to cover real costs is judged differently by scholars.
lessons.riba__two-kinds:
Riba has two forms, and it helps to know both — they show up in different moments.

The first is riba of debt. This is the one everyone already knows about: someone lends money, and asks for extra back just for the waiting. Say a friend lends you $10 and expects $12 back next week — that extra $2 for nothing but time is this kind of riba. It's the same idea behind credit card interest that piles up if you don't pay in full, or a savings account that pays you extra just for leaving money sitting there, or a late fee that grows every day you're overdue.

The second is riba of exchange. This one is sneakier. It happens when you swap two amounts of the *same* kind of valuable thing, but unequally, or with a delay. An old hadith names six things this rule applies to: gold, silver, wheat, barley, dates, and salt. The rule is simple — if you're trading one of these for the exact same thing, it has to be equal amounts, handed over on the spot. So you couldn't trade 10 grams of gold jewelry for 12 grams of gold jewelry, even if yours is nicer quality. Instead, you'd sell your gold for money, then use that money to buy the other gold.

Here's the part people forget: this also applies to currency exchange. Say you're changing pocket money from one currency to another before a trip. That's allowed, at the going rate — but both sides need to hand over their money right away, in the same transaction. If one side pays now and the other promises to pay later, that delay itself turns it into riba.

The second type can feel far removed from everyday life, but it's actually the reason Islamic financial institutions structure their deals around buying and selling real, physical things — instead of just lending money and charging extra for it.
lessons.riba__way-out:
Finding out that some of your money is tangled up with riba — that extra amount added on top of a loan, like paying back more than you borrowed just because time passed — isn't a disaster. It's actually the moment things start getting better. The message here is simple: stop what's still going on, don't torture yourself over what already happened.

So what do you actually do?

First, stop anything new. If you're being offered a new card that adds interest, or a savings account that promises "extra money for free" just for keeping your cash there, don't sign up. Adding more of the same problem while trying to clean up the old one doesn't really work.

Second, get the full picture. Write down exactly what's out there — how much, at what extra rate, for how long. It sounds boring, but not knowing the real numbers is often the exact thing that keeps people stuck and avoiding it.

Third, deal with the most expensive one first. If you owe money in a few places, pay off the one with the highest extra charge before the others. The math is simple: the higher the rate, the faster it grows, so ignoring it the longest costs you the most.

Fourth — what about money you already received this way? Say a savings account already added some "bonus" interest to your balance. Scholars generally agree you shouldn't keep that extra bit for yourself, like spending it on something you want. The common view is to give that amount away for the good of others, not as a reward-earning act of charity, but simply as a way of cleaning your money. The exact method is worth asking a knowledgeable person about directly.

Fifth, don't try to figure out a messy real-life situation alone — a mortgage, an inheritance, a business that's partly tied to interest. These get complicated fast, and general rules don't replace someone actually listening to your specific case. Find someone knowledgeable and explain the details.

One last thing worth saying honestly: fear and embarrassment make people put this off for years, while the amount owed just keeps growing. Facing it early, even if it feels uncomfortable now, is always easier than facing it later.
lessons.riba__what-is-riba:
Imagine a friend asks to borrow $10 from you, and you say, "Fine, but next week you give me back $11." That extra dollar isn't payment for anything you did — you didn't work for it, you didn't risk anything, you just handed over money and demanded more back. That extra dollar is riba.

It doesn't matter what you call it — a "fee," a "thank-you gift," "interest for waiting." The name doesn't change what's really happening: money grew just because it was lent, not because of any real effort or risk.

Why does this matter so much? Think about someone who saves up birthday money and buys candy to resell at school. They're taking a real risk — maybe nobody buys it, maybe it melts, maybe they lose money. That risk is why any profit they make is fair and earned.

Riba has no risk at all. The person lending money gets their extra amount back no matter what — even if the borrower is struggling and has nothing left. All the risk sits on the person who needed help in the first place, while the one who already had extra money keeps getting more. That's why this is treated so seriously — it takes from people who are in need and gives more to people who already have plenty.

It's not only about the person receiving the extra money, either. According to a hadith, the one who takes riba, the one who pays it, the one who writes down the agreement, and even the two witnesses to it are all treated the same. So just helping set up a deal like that counts too — not only profiting from it.

One important thing to be clear about: this isn't about profit being bad. Earning money by selling something honestly, renting things out, or investing together and sharing the risk — all of that is completely fine, even encouraged. The problem isn't making money. It's making money with zero risk, off someone else's need.
lessons.zakat-basics__eight-categories:
Zakat doesn't just go to anyone you feel like helping. Allah lists exactly eight groups of people who can receive it, right there in the Quran. It's not a "here are some ideas" list — it's the whole list. Nothing outside it counts.

Here's who they are:

- People who are poor — they don't have enough to cover basic needs.
- People who are even worse off than that, barely getting by at all.
- People who do the actual work of collecting and handing out zakat — they get paid for that job from the zakat itself.
- People whose hearts need bringing closer, like someone who just became Muslim and is going through a hard time.
- Freeing people from being trapped or enslaved — historically this meant buying someone's freedom, and scholars today apply it to helping people out of forced, unfree situations.
- People crushed by debt they genuinely can't pay off.
- A category connected to "the path of Allah" — scholars don't fully agree on how wide this one is.
- A traveler who's stuck somewhere with no money, even if they're actually well-off back home.

Now, who doesn't get zakat:

- People you're already responsible for feeding and housing — your parents, your kids, your spouse. Taking care of them is your job anyway, separate from zakat.
- Anyone who's already comfortable financially and doesn't fit into any of the eight groups above.
- Most scholars say descendants of the Prophet ﷺ's family shouldn't receive zakat at all.

Here's something nice, though: if your cousin, aunt, or older brother is struggling and you're not already required to support them, giving them zakat isn't just allowed — it's actually better than giving to a stranger. You're helping someone in need and strengthening family ties at the same time.

This is also exactly why AM Network checks things the way it does. Every case gets compared against these eight categories from the Quran, and someone real — an imam, a volunteer, someone from a partner organization — confirms on the ground that the person actually exists and actually needs it.
lessons.zakat-basics__nisab:
Imagine you're saving money in a jar or on a bank card — birthday gifts, allowance, maybe money from a small side job. At what point does zakat (the giving that's required, not just kind to do) actually kick in? That's what nisab answers.

Nisab is a line in the sand. Below it, you don't owe anything at all. This isn't a trick to squeeze money out of you — it's actually protection. Zakat is only meant to come from people who have extra, not from someone who's barely managing.

So how is that line measured? Scholars set it using two metals: 85 grams of gold, or 595 grams of silver. You take today's market price of that metal and turn it into an amount in your own currency. That's why the exact number changes from year to year — gold and silver prices move.

Here's something worth knowing: gold and silver give pretty different amounts, and right now the silver line is much lower than the gold one. Some scholars calculate using gold, others using silver. Many scholars and charities today prefer the silver amount, simply because it's lower — more people end up owing zakat, which means more help reaches people who need it. This isn't one side being "right" and the other "wrong" — it's a genuinely accepted difference of opinion.

There's a second condition too, called hawl. Your savings need to sit at or above the nisab line for a full lunar year — about 354 days. The clock starts the day you first hit the nisab. And if your savings dip below the line sometime during the year but climb back up by the end, most scholars say the year still counts — what matters is where you started and where you ended up, not every wobble in between.

In practice, it's simple: pick one date on the lunar calendar and check your savings on that same date every year. A lot of people choose Ramadan, just because it's easy to remember.
lessons.zakat-basics__what-counts:
Zakat isn't charged on everything you own. The rule is simple: if the money or stuff can grow, or if it's just sitting there piling up as savings, it counts. If you're actually using it to live your life, it doesn't.

So what counts?

- Cash — in your wallet, on a bank card, in a savings jar under your bed.
- Gold and silver — coins, jewelry, anything like that.
- Stuff you bought to resell — say you buy phone cases cheap and sell them for more. You count them at what they're worth right now, not what you paid.
- Investments — stocks, shares, digital assets like crypto, if you have any of that.
- Money someone owes you — if your friend borrowed some of your savings and you genuinely expect them to pay it back.

What doesn't count? Basically, the things you use, not save:

- The house you live in, your clothes, your furniture, your plates and cups.
- Your bike or your family's car — whatever you actually drive or ride.
- Tools you use to earn money. A carpenter's saw, a programmer's laptop, a taxi driver's car — these are work tools, not savings.
- A shop's building and equipment don't count either — only the goods sitting on the shelves waiting to be sold do.

Before you calculate anything, you're allowed to subtract debts you owe — especially ones that are already due. So if you owe someone money and it's time to pay it back, that amount comes off your total first.

There's one point people genuinely disagree on: jewelry a woman wears regularly, not saved up as treasure. One school of thought (Hanafi) says gold and silver jewelry always counts, no matter what it's used for. Many scholars from other schools say normal, reasonably-sized jewelry that's actually worn doesn't count, only if it's being hoarded as savings. This is an old, respected disagreement — not something this lesson can settle for you. Worth asking a knowledgeable person which view to follow.

Whatever counts in the end, the rate is always the same: 2.5%, or one fortieth of the total.
lessons.zakat-basics__what-is-zakat:
Zakat is the third pillar of Islam. If your savings reach a certain amount, giving zakat isn't something extra you choose to do — it's something you're required to do.

It helps to think about what the word "zakat" actually means: it means both "purifying" and "growing." When you give it, you clean the rest of your money, and you clean your heart from being too attached to what you own.

Now, how is this different from sadaqah, regular charity? Say you give a few dollars to a classmate who forgot their lunch money, or drop some coins in a donation box — that's sadaqah. You choose to do it, you choose the amount, you choose who gets it, and nothing bad happens if you don't. Zakat isn't like that. It has an exact rate — 2.5% of what you've saved up — clear rules about who has to pay it, and a specific list of people (set out in the Quran) who receive it. Skipping zakat when you owe it is a sin. Skipping sadaqah is not.

Here's the part that surprises people: zakat isn't taken from what you earn, but from what you keep. Imagine you get pocket money every week, or a gift of cash from a relative on Eid. If you spend it — on snacks, games, whatever — there's nothing left to pay zakat on. But if you keep saving it, in a jar or on a bank card, and a full year passes with that amount still sitting there above the threshold, that's when zakat becomes due. Someone could earn a lot of money in a year, but if they spend it all and have nothing left over the threshold by year's end, they owe no zakat — because zakat isn't a tax on income, it's a small share owed on what's been sitting untouched, growing, for a year.
lessons.zakat-sadaqah-waqf__sadaqah:
Садака doesn't have to mean money. There's a hadith that says every joint in your body should give садака every day the sun rises — and then it lists things that cost nothing: settling a fair argument between two people, helping someone carry something heavy, saying a kind word, walking to prayer, moving something dangerous off the path. So even if your pocket money jar is empty this week, you're not shut out of giving.

When money is involved, the Quran describes it growing like a single grain that turns into seven ears, with a hundred grains on each ear. One small thing you give can end up counting far more than the amount itself.

But there's something that cancels садака out just as clearly: reminding someone what you gave them, or making them feel small about it. Say you gave a classmate some of your lunch money and later bring it up to make them feel bad — the Quran treats that kind of guilt-tripping as seriously as showing off when you give. It ruins the whole thing.

That's why quiet giving is preferred. Giving openly can be good — it might inspire others to give too. But giving quietly, so the person receiving doesn't feel embarrassed, is described as better. It protects their dignity and keeps your own intention clean.

There's also садака джария — giving that keeps working after you're gone. A hadith says a person's good deeds stop when they die, except three: садака that keeps benefiting people, knowledge that people still use, and a righteous child who prays for them.

This changes how you think about giving. Handing someone lunch money solves today's problem. But something like teaching a younger kid to read, or a tool that keeps getting used, keeps giving on its own, long after you've stopped thinking about it. That idea is exactly where вакф comes from — that's the next lesson.
lessons.zakat-sadaqah-waqf__three-forms:
Money can leave your hands in three different ways. They look similar from the outside — you give something away — but the rules behind each one are different.

**Zakat** is not a choice. If your savings have sat above a certain amount (called nisab) for a full lunar year, you owe 2.5% of it. Not 2%, not 3% — exactly that. And you can't just hand it to anyone you like. The Quran names eight specific groups of people who can receive it, and that list is closed. Once you give it, it's gone for good — it belongs to the receiver completely.

**Sadaqah** is different. It's a gift you choose to give. Any amount, any time, to anyone who needs it. Say you saved up birthday money in a jar and decide to give some to a classmate whose family is struggling — that's sadaqah. And according to many hadiths, even a kind word or a smile counts as sadaqah, not just money. Like zakat, once given, it's gone — it now belongs to the other person.

**Waqf** works completely differently. Imagine your uncle buys a small orchard and declares it waqf: the orchard itself can never be sold, given away, or passed down as inheritance. It's frozen, forever. What gets given out is only the fruit — literally or as money from selling the fruit — again and again, year after year. You're not giving away the tree. You're giving away everything it will ever produce.

Here's the rule people mess up the most: **sadaqah never replaces zakat**. You could give away ten times what your zakat would have been — birthday money, allowance, gifts — and still owe zakat, untouched. Why? Because zakat has to be given *as zakat*: with that intention, to someone from those eight groups. Being generous in general doesn't cancel a specific debt.

The reverse is also true: zakat is the minimum, not the finish line. The Quran says you won't reach real goodness until you give from what you actually love — not just spare change you won't miss. That's talking about sadaqah, about going beyond what's required.

And there's a contrast worth remembering: the Quran says Allah destroys the growth that comes from riba (a way of gaining money on debt, discussed elsewhere) but makes charity grow. Two opposite directions for the same thing called "money."
lessons.zakat-sadaqah-waqf__waqf:
Imagine you had a goat that gave milk every day. You could sell the goat for quick cash — or you could keep the goat and give away the milk, forever. The goat keeps working. That's the whole idea behind waqf.

It started with a real question. Umar had gotten the best piece of land he'd ever owned, in a place called Khaybar, and he didn't know what to do with something that good. He was told: keep the land itself, don't sell it, don't give it away, don't let anyone inherit it — just give away what it produces. So he did exactly that. The land stayed frozen, untouchable, forever. The harvest went to poor people, relatives, freeing people from slavery, and travelers who needed help.

That's the whole structure, and it's actually simple:

- The **body** (the land, the goat, the thing itself) — never touched, never sold, frozen forever.
- The **fruit** (the milk, the harvest, the rent) — given away, exactly the way the person who set it up said to.

This idea built real things over centuries: free wells, free hospitals, libraries, places for travelers to rest, even universities that ran for hundreds of years — not because someone kept donating, but because the original "goat" kept producing milk on its own.

Here's the part that matters a lot: once someone sets the rule, that rule sticks. If a person said "the income goes to educating orphans," nobody managing it later gets to say "actually I think this other cause is more useful" and switch it. The person's condition is binding — like an agreement everyone has to keep.

Today waqf can look like property, rental income, or a share in a business. There's also the idea of a **money waqf** — where instead of land, you freeze a sum of money, invest it, and give away only what it earns. Many scholars, including in the Hanafi tradition, accept this, though not everyone agrees, so it stays an open question rather than a settled one.

Why bring this up in a lesson about what we're building? Because waqf has historically broken in one specific spot: the person managing it. Conditions get forgotten, land quietly gets sold, income drifts to the wrong place — and a hundred years later, nobody can check what really happened. A smart contract is good at exactly the thing waqf needs: locking a rule so it can't be changed, and sending the income automatically, without depending on someone's good intentions. We haven't launched this yet — the contracts exist but aren't live. But that one property, not any trend around blockchain, is why we chose this path.
